section.title: John's Testimony and the First Disciples
section.sectionRationale: After the prologue, the Gospel's narrative begins with testimony. John the Baptist tells the delegation from Jerusalem who he is not and who he is, a voice pointing away from himself to One already standing among them. He names Jesus the Lamb of God. Then, over a handful of days, the first disciples are drawn in, one bringing another, and a cascade of titles piles up: Rabbi, Messiah, Son of God, King of Israel, Son of Man.
section.thesis: The forerunner points away from himself to Jesus, the Lamb of God who takes away the sin of the world, and as the first disciples come and see, they discover Him to be the Messiah, the Son of God, and the Son of Man on whom heaven itself is opened.
section.frameNote: Four movements: John's answer to the delegation, I am not the Christ but a voice; John's declaration, Look, the Lamb of God; the first two disciples who come and see and bring others; and the calling of Philip and Nathanael, ending with the promise of an open heaven.

units.label: The witness before the delegation
units.note: I am not the Christ, but a voice

verses.text: And this was John’s {{martyria|testimony}} when the Jews of Jerusalem sent priests and Levites to ask him, “Who are you?”
He did not refuse to confess, but openly declared, “I am not the Christ.”
“Then who are you?” they inquired. “Are you Elijah?” He said, “I am not.” “Are you the Prophet?” He answered, “No.”
So they said to him, “Who are you? We need an answer for those who sent us. What do you say about yourself?”
John replied in the words of Isaiah the prophet: “I am a voice of one calling in the wilderness, ‘Make straight the way for the Lord.’”
Then the Pharisees who had been sent
asked him, “Why then do you baptize, if you are not the Christ, nor Elijah, nor the Prophet?”
“I baptize with water,” John replied, “but among you stands One you do not know.
He is the One who comes after me, the straps of whose sandals I am not worthy to untie.”
All this happened at Bethany beyond the Jordan, where John was baptizing.

units.label: Behold, the Lamb of God
units.note: who takes away the sin of the world

verses.text: The next day John saw Jesus coming toward him and said, “Look, the {{amnos|Lamb of God}}, who takes away the sin of the world!
This is He of whom I said, ‘A man who comes after me has surpassed me because He was before me.’
I myself did not know Him, but the reason I came baptizing with water was that He might be revealed to Israel.”
Then John testified, “I saw the Spirit descending from heaven like a dove and resting on Him.
I myself did not know Him, but the One who sent me to baptize with water told me, ‘The man on whom you see the Spirit descend and rest is He who will baptize with the Holy Spirit.’
I have seen and testified that this is the Son of God.”

units.label: Come and see
units.note: the first disciples follow and bring others

verses.text: The next day John was there again with two of his disciples.
When he saw Jesus walking by, he said, “Look, the Lamb of God!”
And when the two disciples heard him say this, they followed Jesus.
Jesus turned and saw them following. “What do you want?” He asked. They said to Him, “Rabbi” (which means Teacher), “where are You staying?”
“Come and see,” He replied. So they went and saw where He was staying, and spent that day with Him. It was about the tenth hour.
Andrew, Simon Peter’s brother, was one of the two who heard John’s testimony and followed Jesus.
He first found his brother Simon and told him, “We have found the {{Messias|Messiah}}” (which is translated as Christ).
Andrew brought him to Jesus, who looked at him and said, “You are Simon son of John. You will be called Cephas” (which is translated as Peter).
The next day Jesus decided to set out for Galilee. Finding Philip, He told him, “Follow Me.”
Now Philip was from Bethsaida, the same town as Andrew and Peter.
Philip found Nathanael and told him, “We have found the One Moses wrote about in the Law, the One the prophets foretold, Jesus of Nazareth, the son of Joseph.”
“Can anything good come from Nazareth?” Nathanael asked. “Come and see,” said Philip.
When Jesus saw Nathanael approaching, He said of him, “Here is a true Israelite, in whom there is no deceit.”
“How do You know me?” Nathanael asked. Jesus replied, “Before Philip called you, I saw you under the fig tree.”
“Rabbi,” Nathanael answered, “You are the Son of God! You are the King of Israel!”
Jesus said to him, “Do you believe just because I told you I saw you under the fig tree? You will see greater things than these.”
Then He declared, “Truly, truly, I tell you, you will all see heaven open and the angels of God ascending and descending on the {{huiosanthropou|Son of Man}}.”

martyria.gloss: Testimony, witness, evidence given. Witness is a major theme in John; the Baptist, the works, the Scriptures, the Father, and the Spirit all bear testimony to Jesus. John's own testimony is a model of true witness: it does not draw attention to itself but points wholly to Christ. The related word gives us the term martyr.

amnos.gloss: Lamb. The Baptist calls Jesus the Lamb of God who takes away the sin of the world, gathering up the Passover lamb whose blood shielded Israel and the lamb led to slaughter in Isaiah 53. It announces from the start that this Messiah has come to die as a sacrifice, bearing away sin, a theme the Gospel drives toward the cross at Passover.

Messias.gloss: Messiah, the Anointed One, transliterated from Hebrew and rendered in Greek as Christos, Christ. It names the long-promised king from David's line whom God would send to rescue and rule His people. Andrew's cry, we have found the Messiah, announces that the age of promise has arrived in Jesus.

huiosanthropou.gloss: Son of Man, Jesus' favored self-designation, drawn from Daniel 7, where one like a son of man is given everlasting dominion and comes on the clouds. In John the title also marks the one who descends and ascends, the meeting point of heaven and earth. The promise of an open heaven over the Son of Man recalls Jacob's ladder, Genesis 28.

basic.context: The story proper opens with John the Baptist under questioning from a delegation of priests and Levites. He clears the ground by saying who he is not, not the Christ, not Elijah, not the Prophet, and who he is, only a voice preparing the way. Then he points to Jesus and calls Him the Lamb of God who takes away the world's sin. Over the next few days the first disciples come to Jesus, and each one brings someone else: Andrew brings Simon, Philip brings Nathanael. The passage ends with Jesus promising an open heaven.
basic.hermeneutics: Watch two things. First, the pattern of true witness: John constantly deflects attention from himself to Christ, a model for every believer. Second, the piling up of titles, Lamb of God, Rabbi, Messiah, Son of God, King of Israel, Son of Man. The key question is whether we will do what the first disciples did, come and see, and follow. The invitation come and see is how faith begins.
basic.originalLanguages: The section turns on witness, martyria, John's testimony that points only to Jesus. The great title is the amnos, the Lamb of God, announcing a sacrifice for sin. Andrew announces the Messias, the Messiah, the promised King. And Jesus crowns the titles with Son of Man, huios tou anthropou, over whom heaven is opened.
basic.typology: The Lamb of God gathers up the Passover lamb and the suffering servant of Isaiah 53. The open heaven and the angels ascending and descending on the Son of Man recall Jacob's ladder at Bethel; Jesus Himself is now the stairway between heaven and earth.
basic.christ: Every title in the passage lands on Jesus. He is the Lamb who bears away sin, the Messiah long promised, the Son of God, the King of Israel, and the Son of Man who joins heaven and earth. The forerunner's whole ministry exists to point to Him, and the first disciples' whole future begins by following Him.
basic.god: God is the one who sends: He sends John to bear witness, He reveals the sign of the Spirit descending, and He gives the promised Messiah. He is a God who initiates, seeking and calling people, and who keeps the promises of the prophets in sending His Lamb and King.
basic.crossReferences: Isaiah 40 supplies the voice in the wilderness. Isaiah 53 stands behind the Lamb who bears sin. Genesis 28 lies behind the open heaven and the angels on the Son of Man. Daniel 7 gives the Son of Man His dominion.
basic.oneStory: The promises are converging. The forerunner announced by Isaiah appears, points to the Lamb foreshadowed at Passover and in Isaiah 53, and the first followers recognize the Messiah of David's line. Jesus reveals Himself as the Son of Man of Daniel and the true ladder of Bethel, the one in whom heaven is opened to earth.

context.literary:
John 1:19 is a hinge. The prologue, verses 1 to 18, spoke in the language of eternity; from here the Gospel counts days. The delegation comes on one day, 'the next day' brings the pointing finger of verse 29, 'the next day' again verse 35, and 'the next day' once more verse 43. Then chapter 2 opens 'on the third day.' Reckon from verse 43 and the wedding at Cana lands on the seventh day of the sequence. Many readers hear a new creation week, with the Word who made all things now walking a Galilean road. That is an inference, but the careful tallying of days is the author's own doing, and he does nothing like it again until the final week before the cross.

Within the days the writing is built on echoing words. The verb for testify and its noun run through every scene: John testifies about the light, 1:7, to the delegation, 1:19, and about the Spirit, 1:32 and 34, and the section ends with Nathanael testifying in his turn. The word for 'remain' (meno) quietly links the Spirit who rests on Jesus, verses 32 and 33, with the two men who ask where He is 'staying' and then spend the day with Him, verses 38 and 39. 'Come and see' is spoken twice, by Jesus in verse 39 and by Philip in verse 46, so the first invitation is passed hand to hand.

The scene also has a deliberate shape in its denials and confessions. John answers three questions with a short refusal, 'I am not,' 'I am not,' 'No,' in verses 20 and 21, and the Gospel makes sure we hear the emphasis, since verse 20 says he 'did not refuse to confess, but openly declared.' By contrast, the disciples' confessions grow upward: Rabbi, Messiah, the One of whom Moses wrote, Son of God, King of Israel, and finally Jesus' own title for Himself, Son of Man. Notice too that the Gospel records no baptism of Jesus. John reports only what he saw afterward, so the weight falls on testimony rather than on the event.
context.historical:
The delegation of priests and Levites came from Jerusalem, so the temple establishment itself was sending investigators out to the Jordan. Priests tended the sacrifices and Levites served as temple police and singers; a baptizing prophet drawing crowds beyond their control was exactly what they would need to assess. The Jewish historian Josephus, writing later, also describes John as a popular preacher who called people to righteousness and baptism, which fits the picture of a movement large enough to alarm the authorities.

The questions asked are a map of the hopes of the day. Malachi 4:5 promised Elijah before the great and terrible day of the LORD, and the Prophet of Deuteronomy 18:15 was another figure of expectation, sometimes held apart from the Messiah. 'Christ' is the Greek rendering of the Hebrew mashiach, 'anointed one,' the title of Israel's kings. John's baptizing in the Jordan stirred memory of the nation crossing into the land under Joshua, and washing with water was already familiar to Jews as a cleansing from impurity and, for converts from the nations, as entry into the covenant people. What shocked was that John called born Israelites to a baptism of repentance.

Isaiah 40:3 was read by some in that period as a call to go out to the desert and prepare. The Qumran community, for example, applied it to its own withdrawal into the wilderness. John, by contrast, reads it as a call to announce the arrival of someone, which is why he quotes it as a voice rather than as a program.

The setting of the second half is Galilean. Bethsaida, home of Andrew, Peter and Philip, was a fishing town on the northern shore of the lake, and John 12:21 calls it 'Bethsaida in Galilee.' Nazareth, by contrast, was a small village in the hills never mentioned in the Old Testament, which gives Nathanael's jibe its sting. The 'tenth hour' of verse 39 is most naturally four in the afternoon by the Jewish count from sunrise, though a few hold that John uses a Roman count and means ten in the morning. Either way, a day was spent with Him.
context.canonical:
John's testimony takes up the prophet of the wilderness. Isaiah 40:3 opens the second half of Isaiah with comfort for exiles and a highway for God's own return, and all four Gospels apply it to the Baptist. Only John has the Baptist himself speak the words, as a self-description rather than an editorial note. The text is also quoted in the other Gospels at the opening of Mark 1:2-3 alongside Malachi 3:1, so that the forerunner is set at the head of the entire Gospel story.

The Lamb of verse 29 gathers a long line of sacrificial pictures. Abraham told Isaac that God would provide the lamb, Genesis 22:8; the Passover lamb's blood marked Israelite doors, Exodus 12:13; the servant is led like a lamb to the slaughter, Isaiah 53:7. The Fourth Gospel returns to this at the end, where Jesus is condemned on the day of preparation for the Passover, John 19:14, and a bone of His is not broken, John 19:36, matching Exodus 12:46. Paul says plainly that 'Christ, our Passover lamb, has been sacrificed,' 1 Corinthians 5:7, and Peter speaks of 'the precious blood of Christ, a lamb without blemish or spot,' 1 Peter 1:19. Revelation then makes the Lamb the central figure of heaven's worship, Revelation 5:6 and 5:12.

The Spirit who descends and remains recalls Isaiah 11:2, where the Spirit rests on the shoot from Jesse's stump, and Isaiah 42:1, where the servant is given the Spirit. Jesus' promise to Nathanael sums up the passage with Genesis 28:12 and Daniel 7:13. Jesus is greater than the place where Jacob dreamed. Later in the Gospel the Son of Man is lifted up, John 3:14 and 12:34, and the angels' going up and down is fulfilled in His ministry rather than in a vision. The movement from Baptist to the first disciples to the great confessions is picked up again at the end of the Gospel, where Thomas confesses 'My Lord and my God,' John 20:28, and the author states his purpose, that readers may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, John 20:31.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
John writes so that his readers will believe, John 20:31, and this scene is the first slow demonstration of how that happens. He wants us to notice that every witness here has a limit. The Baptist cannot give what he points to; he can only say 'Look.' Andrew can only bring his brother, and Philip can only say 'Come and see.' The author deliberately gives the least impressive possible arguments, an invitation and a pointing finger, because the weight sits on the One who is pointed to.

He also wants readers to feel the gap between what people can say and what Jesus is. The titles climb, but the last one, Son of Man, is Jesus' own word, and it is the one with a promise attached: greater things will be seen. The first hearers, probably including Jews and Gentiles who knew the Greek Old Testament, were meant to take a lesson about the shape of faith. It begins with a testimony, takes a risk, spends a day, and ends in a confession that is bigger than the person making it knew.

Finally, John wants readers to hear a challenge dressed as a story. The delegation asks questions and gets answers but does not move. The disciples ask a smaller question, where are You staying, and move in. The reader is asked which kind of listener he is.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The passage describes a unique week. John's role as the last of the prophets, the particular men called, and the sign of the dove descending are not repeated, and nobody today is told to expect an open sky or to be named Cephas. It would also be a mistake to read Jesus' sight of Nathanael under the fig tree as a rule that He will always give a personal word of knowledge in exactly this way.

What is meant to travel is the pattern. A witness points away from himself; an invitation is offered without pressure; a person is allowed to test it by spending time with Jesus; and the one who has found Him tells the next person. The text does not claim that every first encounter will be dramatic. Andrew's approach is quiet, and Philip's is almost casual. It also does not promise that every invitation will be welcomed, for Nathanael's skepticism is voiced openly and is not scolded. 'Come and see' answers prejudice with an offer of evidence, and the passage commends it as a way of speaking about Jesus that remains open to anyone's honest question.

debates.question: When was the 'tenth hour' of verse 39, and does it matter?

views.label: Four in the afternoon by the Jewish count
views.case: Jewish daytime was counted from sunrise, so the first hour was about six and the tenth about four. That fits an afternoon encounter, with the day nearly over, so that 'spent that day with Him' means they stayed into the evening.

views.label: Ten in the morning by a Roman civil count
views.case: Some argue John counts hours from midnight, as Roman civil reckoning did, which would make it ten in the morning and leave a whole day for the conversation. They point to the sixth hour in John 19:14 and 4:6 as evidence of a different convention.

debates.bearing: The Gospel gives no sign that the hour matters to the argument, only that the memory was so vivid that someone recalled the time. The point is that two men stayed, and were changed.

debates.question: Who are the 'Jews' and 'Pharisees' of verses 19 and 24, and why are the Pharisees mentioned separately?

views.label: The Jerusalem leadership as a whole
views.case: In John, 'the Jews' very often means the authorities in Judea rather than the Jewish people. The priests and Levites of verse 19 represent the temple establishment, and verse 24 adds the party that cared most about baptism and purity.

views.label: Two delegations, or one with a Pharisaic element
views.case: Verse 24 is grammatically ambiguous: the Greek may say that the envoys were from the Pharisees, or that the Pharisees themselves had been sent. The questions of verse 25 about why John baptizes sound like a legal party asking about the authority for a new rite.

debates.bearing: Either way, the questioners arrive from Jerusalem with official concerns, which is why John's reply is both a refusal of a title and a pointer to One 'among you' they do not know.

debates.question: Why does the Baptist deny that he is Elijah when Jesus later says he is?

views.label: He answers the question asked
views.case: The delegation asks whether he is Elijah returned in person. John rightly says no, and Jesus later says only that John is the Elijah who was to come, Matthew 11:14, in the sense of fulfilling the role of Malachi 4:5.

views.label: John is modest, and the Gospel keeps the focus on Christ
views.case: John refuses every title that might draw attention to himself. The Fourth Gospel never says he is Elijah, because its aim is to keep John as pure witness.

debates.bearing: The two statements do not conflict: John disowns the person and the position, while Jesus affirms the function. That John answered with Isaiah rather than Malachi shows how he understood himself.

study.originalLanguages:
Start with the verb for 'takes away' in verse 29, airo. It can mean to lift up and to carry off, and in this verse it is a present participle, 'the One who takes away,' as though the work is ongoing and characteristic of Him. John 1 does not choose between 'bears' and 'removes'; the same verb is used in 1 John 3:5, 'He appeared to take away sins.' The object is the singular 'sin of the world,' not a list of sins. John is not describing a response to one particular fault, but to the burden as a whole, and the whole world is its scope. When the Septuagint renders the lamb of Isaiah 53:7 it uses amnos, the same word as here, and the suffering servant there 'bears' the sins of many, Isaiah 53:12. That is a strong verbal reason to hear Isaiah, though the Passover animal in Exodus 12 is not called amnos in the Greek Old Testament, so the link to the Passover is made by theme and by John's own later timeline rather than by this word.

A second thread is the verb meno, 'remain.' The Spirit descends 'and remained' on Him, verses 32 and 33, which marks Jesus out as the permanent bearer of the Spirit, unlike prophets on whom the Spirit came for a time. Then the two disciples ask 'where are You staying,' and the verb is the same, as is the day they 'stayed,' verse 39. In this Gospel meno becomes the vocabulary of abiding, as in John 15:4. A sharp reader hears that the disciples' question is already more than an inquiry about lodging.

Third, notice 'Look' in verses 29 and 36. It is the imperative ide, the same word Philip uses in verse 46 as 'see.' The Baptist points, and Philip invites, using the same verb. The experience of 'seeing' is the Gospel's way of speaking about faith, since the verbs of sight and testimony keep returning together.

Fourth, the names. 'Messiah' is given in verse 41 as the Greek 'Messias,' a transliteration of the Aramaic that John then glosses as Christ. The word appears in the New Testament only here and at John 4:25, in the mouth of the Samaritan woman, and so frames the first great acts of recognition by a disciple and an outsider. 'Cephas' is Aramaic for 'rock,' and Peter, Petros, is the Greek form. The change of name belongs to the pattern in which God renames people to match a calling, as with Abram and Jacob.

Last, 'in whom there is no deceit,' verse 47. The word is dolos, and the note carries a quiet allusion. Jacob, later named Israel, was the one who in Genesis 27:35 'came deceitfully,' and Nathanael is called a true Israelite, free of that trait. The Gospel often uses double meaning, and a name with a story behind it is part of the method.

typology.fulfillment: Jacob, fleeing his brother, dreamed of a stairway with angels going up and down, and woke saying 'this is the gate of heaven.' Jesus tells Nathanael that the angels will ascend and descend 'on the Son of Man,' placing Himself where the ladder stood. The correspondence is deliberate, given that Nathanael has just been called a true Israelite, a man of Jacob's line without Jacob's deceit. The escalation is that the meeting place is no longer a stone pillar in the desert but a person, so that access to heaven is found in Him. The type falls short because Jacob only saw a dream, while the Gospel records that heaven's work flows through the Son of Man on earth, and finally lifts Him up, John 3:14.

typology.type: The Passover lamb and the lamb of the servant, Exodus 12 and Isaiah 53
typology.fulfillment: The Passover lamb's blood marked a household so that judgment passed over, Exodus 12:13, and the servant of Isaiah is led like a lamb to the slaughter, Isaiah 53:7. John's Gospel ties the two to the cross: Jesus dies at the hour the lambs were being killed, John 19:14, and a bone of His is not broken, matching Exodus 12:46, John 19:36. Paul states the correspondence, 1 Corinthians 5:7. The escalation is scale and finality: the old lamb protected one nation for a night, but this Lamb takes away the sin of the world. The type falls short because animal sacrifices were repeated, while this offering was made once, Hebrews 10:11-12.

typology.type: The Spirit descending and remaining, Isaiah 11:2 and the servant
typology.fulfillment: Isaiah foresaw a shoot from Jesse on whom the Spirit would rest, Isaiah 11:2, and a servant on whom God's Spirit was put, Isaiah 42:1. John sees that promise happen, and the sign he was told to watch for identifies the One who baptizes with the Holy Spirit. The escalation is that the Anointed One is not only given the Spirit but is the giver of the Spirit to others, a promise that begins to be realized at Pentecost, Acts 2:33. The type falls short in that earlier anointed figures, such as kings and prophets, received the Spirit for tasks, while Jesus receives Him without limit, John 3:34.

Philip tells Nathanael that Jesus is the One of whom Moses wrote, which draws on the promise of a prophet like Moses. Moses spoke God's words to Israel and mediated a covenant at the mountain. Jesus speaks what He has seen with the Father, and John 6:14 later reports that people recognized Him as 'the Prophet who is to come into the world.' The escalation is from servant to Son, Hebrews 3:5-6. The correspondence stops short of making Jesus merely a second Moses, since the Gospel says the Law came through Moses but grace and truth came through Jesus Christ, John 1:17.

study.christ:
The passage leads to Christ by direct witness first. Almost nothing here is hidden typology; John says plainly who Jesus is. What deserves attention is what the testimonies add up to. The Baptist says that the One who comes after him ranks before him, 'because He was before me,' verse 30, which looks back to the prologue's claim that the Word was in the beginning. A man who comes later in time is first in being. The Lamb, then, is not a victim chosen from the flock but the pre-existent Son.

The Lamb of God also lifts the question of what sin is. The word in verse 29 is singular and universal, 'the sin of the world,' and the One who removes it is also the One who baptizes with the Holy Spirit, verse 33. Together they say that Jesus deals with guilt and then gives new life. Other Scriptures hold both in view. Paul says that the Son 'bore our sins in His body on the tree,' 1 Peter 2:24, and then that those who are in Him have received the Spirit, Galatians 3:13-14. The two halves of the Baptist's testimony are really the two halves of the gospel: forgiveness and the gift of the Spirit.

The sequence of titles builds a portrait. Rabbi, 'Teacher,' names what he does, but Messiah and Son of God and King of Israel name who He is. Nathanael's confession, 'You are the Son of God! You are the King of Israel!' echoes Psalm 2, where the anointed King is addressed as God's Son, Psalm 2:6-7. Yet Jesus tells him that he will see 'greater things,' and the greater thing is the Son of Man title. In Daniel 7:13-14 the one like a son of man receives an everlasting kingdom, and in John 1:51 the heaven that opens is bound to His person. Where Jacob saw a ladder, the disciples will see the One in whom heaven and earth are joined, John 3:13.

The passage even shows the character of this Christ. He asks 'What do you want?' before He tells anyone anything, verse 38. He invites rather than interrogates, and He gives a day. He knows Nathanael before Nathanael meets Him, verse 48, which anticipates the verse at the end of chapter 2 that says He knew what was in a man. He promises greater things, so He never leaves a confession where it is.

A word of caution. The fig tree, the six days, and the twelve names to come are not codes to be solved. The links here rest on what John says and on the Old Testament texts he makes his characters quote or recall. The Lamb passages and the Son of Man passages interpret each other, and that is as far as the passage itself takes us.
study.god:
This passage shows a God who speaks before anyone asks. The Baptist's mission was given to him by 'the One who sent me,' verse 33, and he was told in advance what to watch for. God is the one who arranges the sign, who chooses the witness, and who arranges that the right man is at the right place. The pattern is that revelation is first God's initiative, and testimony follows, rather than the other way round.

He is also a God who keeps the long promises of the prophets and does so with surprising precision. Isaiah's voice, Malachi's forerunner, the prophet like Moses, the Lamb of Isaiah 53, the royal Son of Psalm 2, and the Son of Man of Daniel 7 are not scattered scenes. They are brought into one week, and the passage insists that God has been preparing this for centuries. For worship, this means that Israel's Scriptures are not an unfinished tale; they are a promise God has been faithful to.

The passage shows God as a Trinity in action without announcing the doctrine. The Father sends the witness and speaks the word about the Spirit; the Spirit descends and remains on the Son; the Son is the one who baptizes with the Holy Spirit. Nobody here defines the Trinity, but three persons are plainly present, distinguished and acting together, and the Father's act and the Spirit's act both point to the Son.

A tension is held in the text. God is utterly holy, so that sin must be 'taken away' by a sacrifice, yet He is also the one who provides it. In Genesis 22:8 Abraham said God would provide the lamb, and John says that He has. The One who judges sin is the One who bears it; justice and love are not set against each other but met in the Lamb. Equally, God is sovereign in revelation, since the disciples did not find Jesus by their own cleverness, but He is also respectful of human search. 'What do you want?' and 'Come and see' show a God who does not overwhelm people into belief but lets them come close.

For worship, the passage teaches a pattern of response. We worship the One whose own forerunner insisted that he was not worthy to untie His sandal, verse 27, and we worship by pointing away from ourselves. We can also worship with confidence that we are known before we know, as Nathanael was, since God sees us before we are called.

crossReferences.note: The text John quotes of himself. It comes at the start of the comfort section of Isaiah, where the exiles are told that God is coming Himself to His people. By applying it to his own ministry, John says that the God of Isaiah's promise is about to be seen in the person he is pointing to.

The servant who is led like a lamb to the slaughter and does not open his mouth. The Greek Old Testament's word for lamb here is the same word John uses in 1:29, which is among the strongest verbal links between the Baptist's cry and the servant who bears the sins of many.

The Passover rule that no bone of the lamb may be broken. John 19:36 quotes the principle when the soldiers leave Jesus' legs unbroken, so the opening cry about the Lamb is closed at the cross by a physical detail the Gospel treats as fulfillment.

Abraham tells Isaac that God Himself will provide the lamb for the offering. John's Baptist announces that God has done exactly that, which turns an old, unanswered line of faith into a present reality, with the difference that now the substitute is the Son.

The promise of a prophet like Moses, which lies behind the delegation's question and Philip's claim that Moses wrote about Jesus. John answers 'No' to the question, and the Gospel takes the promise as fulfilled in another.

The promise of Elijah before the day of the LORD, the reason a delegation asks whether John is he. John's denial and Jesus' later words in Matthew 11:14 show two sides of one truth: the forerunner was not Elijah in person, but he fulfilled Elijah's task.

Jacob's dream of a stairway set on earth and reaching heaven, with angels going up and down. Jesus gives the image to Nathanael in verse 51, placing the Son of Man where the ladder stood and so announcing Himself as the means of access between God and people.

The vision of one like a son of man approaching the Ancient of Days and receiving a kingdom that never ends. The title Jesus takes for Himself in John 1:51 draws on that picture of authority, and the open heaven suggests the audience in which that authority is exercised.

The anointed King installed on Zion and addressed as God's Son. Nathanael's pairing of Son of God and King of Israel in verse 49 reproduces the pairing, so that his confession, though it is made by a skeptic from a small village, uses the royal vocabulary of the psalms.

The author's own statement of purpose, that readers may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God. The titles confessed in chapter 1 are the same words the Gospel ends on, so the whole book is bookended by testimony and confession, each leading to life in His name.

Peter speaks of redemption by the precious blood of Christ as of a lamb without blemish or spot. Written by one of the men called in this section, it shows what the title Lamb of God came to mean in the church's earliest preaching.

study.oneStory:
The Bible's story has been waiting since Genesis 3 for a rescuer and since Genesis 12 for a blessing that reaches the nations. This passage is where that long waiting turns into pointing. After centuries of prophets the story's first human finger points at a person and says 'Look.' What the passage answers from before is the question the whole Old Testament leaves hanging: how can a holy God deal with sin without ending the people He loves? Abraham spoke of a lamb that God would provide, the Passover blood covered the door, the sacrificial system returned each day and each year, and Isaiah saw a servant who would bear the sin of many. John says the lamb has arrived.

It also answers the question of the nations. Israel was chosen to bless the world, but the failure of Israel and the long exile left that mission unfinished. Here the Lamb takes away the sin 'of the world,' and the first disciples are Galileans from the border country, which is the beginning of a widening circle. The call in the Gospel's next chapters reaches a Samaritan woman and a royal official, and the Gospel closes with the commission to go, John 20:21.

It sets up the rest of the Gospel. The Baptist's testimony is the first of many witnesses, including works, Scripture, the Father and the Spirit, John 5:31-39. Jesus' title as Son of Man will resurface at the cross, where He is 'lifted up,' John 3:14 and 12:23-34, and the heaven that opens here will remain open to those who believe. The Spirit who rests on Him will be given to others after His glorification, John 7:39, and the disciples who come and see will be sent to bring others.

The story ends in new creation, and this passage already shows its outline. In Revelation the Lamb stands at the center of God's throne, Revelation 5:6 and 22:1, and the multitude from every nation who worship Him are the answer to the Baptist's 'sin of the world.' The invitation to come and see that was spoken at a Galilean riverbank is the same voice that closes the Bible: 'Come,' Revelation 22:17, so the first conversation and the last call are made in the same words.

quiz.q: How does John the Baptist describe himself to the delegation?

options.text: As a voice calling in the wilderness to prepare the way of the Lord, not the Christ.
options.note: Verse 23 quotes Isaiah 40:3; John points wholly away from himself to Christ.

options.text: As the prophet Elijah returned in person.
options.note: He explicitly denies being Elijah in verse 21.

options.text: As one preparing the way by baptizing with water.
options.note: True of his ministry, but his self-description here is the voice preparing the Lord's way, a role greater than the baptism itself.

options.text: As a teacher gathering his own following.
options.note: John deliberately deflects from himself; he is not building his own following but pointing to Christ.

quiz.q: What does John mean by calling Jesus the Lamb of God?

options.text: Jesus is the sacrifice who takes away the sin of the world, fulfilling the Passover lamb and Isaiah's servant.
options.note: Verse 29 ties the title to bearing away sin, evoking Passover and Isaiah 53.

options.text: Jesus is gentle and harmless like a lamb.
options.note: Gentleness is not the point; the title announces a sacrificial death that removes sin.

options.text: Jesus is a sacrifice whose blood delivers His people.
options.note: True and central, but it narrows to deliverance and omits that He takes away the sin of the world.

options.text: Jesus is simply another prophet sent to Israel.
options.note: The Lamb of God is far more than a prophet; He is the sin-bearing sacrifice.

quiz.q: How do the first disciples come to Jesus in this passage?

options.text: Through personal witness and the invitation to come and see, one bringing another.
options.note: Andrew brings Simon, Philip brings Nathanael; faith spreads by invitation to come and see.

options.text: By Jesus performing miracles that forced them to believe.
options.note: No miracle compels them here; they come through testimony and encounter.

options.text: Because John the Baptist commanded them to leave him.
options.note: John pointed to Jesus, but the disciples followed freely; he did not issue a command to leave.

options.text: By hearing John call Jesus the Lamb of God and then following.
options.note: True for the first two disciples, but the fuller pattern is personal witness and come and see spreading to others.

quiz.q: What does Jesus promise Nathanael he will see?

options.text: Heaven opened and the angels of God ascending and descending on the Son of Man.
options.note: Verse 51 recalls Jacob's ladder; Jesus is the meeting of heaven and earth.

options.text: The literal fig tree miraculously bearing fruit.
options.note: The fig tree was where Jesus saw him, not the object of the promise.

options.text: Greater signs and works than the ones he has just witnessed.
options.note: Jesus does say he will see greater things, but the specific promise is the open heaven over the Son of Man.

options.text: The kingdom of Israel restored to political power.
options.note: Nathanael confessed Jesus as King of Israel, but the promise points to heaven opened, not a political restoration.

quiz.q: What titles are given to Jesus in this passage?

options.text: Lamb of God, Rabbi, Messiah, Son of God, King of Israel, and Son of Man.
options.note: All these titles appear across verses 29 to 51, revealing who Jesus is.

options.text: Only Rabbi and Teacher, ordinary titles of respect.
options.note: Those titles appear, but the passage piles up far higher titles like Lamb of God and Son of Man.

options.text: Messiah, Son of God, and King of Israel.
options.note: These are all present, but the list leaves out the crucial Lamb of God and Son of Man.

options.text: Prophet, priest, and Elijah returned.
options.note: These are not the titles given to Jesus here; Elijah is denied of John, not applied to Jesus.

questions: John the Baptist constantly pointed away from himself to Jesus. Where are you tempted to draw attention to yourself, and what would it look like to be a voice that points to Christ?
Jesus is announced as the Lamb of God who takes away the sin of the world. How does it steady your conscience to know your sin was carried away by Him?
The disciples came because someone said come and see. Who first invited you toward Jesus, and whom might you invite now?
Jesus saw Nathanael under the fig tree before Philip called him. How does it affect you to know that Jesus already sees and knows you before you come to Him?
Andrew's first act was to find his brother Simon. Who is the one person God may be calling you to bring to Jesus?

translationNotes.note: John quotes Isaiah 40:3, a voice of one calling in the wilderness; the BSB footnote points to the passage and its Greek Old Testament form. He applies the forerunner prophecy to himself.
I baptize with water; the BSB footnote notes the preposition can also read in, here and in verses 31 and 33. The contrast is with the One who will baptize with the Holy Spirit.
This is the Son of God; the BSB footnote records a variant, the Chosen One of God, in some manuscripts. Either reading is a high confession of who Jesus is.
Cephas is Aramaic for rock, translated into Greek as Peter; the Gospel explains the name for its readers, as it does with Messiah and Rabbi.
